title: Data Protection Impact Assessment
summary: A Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) is a structured review carried out before processing that is likely to result in a high risk to people's rights and freedoms. It describes the processing, records why it is necessary and proportionate, sets out the risks to individuals, and lists the measures that reduce those risks. That record is then used to decide whether to proceed, change the design, or consult the supervisory authority when significant risk remains. It is a process rather than a document alone, and it has to start early enough to influence the design instead of justifying a finished system. Typical triggers are large scale profiling, systematic monitoring, special category data and the use of new technology. The common mistake is filling in a template after launch, or writing a risk section that names no genuine residual risk, which makes the assessment worthless as evidence of accountability.

exercises.title: Data Protection Impact Assessment - EASY
exercises.summary: Recall and recognition: definitions, one clear answer, single-step questions.

exercises.title: Data Protection Impact Assessment - MEDIUM
exercises.summary: Application: read a short log or alert and choose the correct next step.

exercises.title: Data Protection Impact Assessment - HARD
exercises.summary: Analysis: a multi-step scenario with distractors, evidence to weigh, and a reason to give.

exercises.title: Data Protection Impact Assessment - EXTREMELY HARD
exercises.summary: Synthesis under pressure: incomplete evidence, competing priorities, and a decision you must defend.

beginner.definition: A Data Protection Impact Assessment is a careful check before you start using personal data in a risky way. It describes what you plan to do, why you need it, and what could go wrong for the people involved. You write down the steps you will take to reduce those risks.
beginner.whyItMatters: Some projects can harm people if they go wrong, such as watching behaviour or sorting people into groups. Thinking about that harm early is easier and cheaper than fixing it later. The written record also shows that you took your duties seriously. If the risk stays high after your fixes, you may need to ask a regulator before you continue. Skipping the assessment can lead to fines, lost trust and a project that must be rebuilt.
howItWorks: You describe the project, the data it uses and the purpose behind it.
You explain why the project is needed and whether a gentler option exists.
You list the risks to the people whose data you will use.
You choose measures that reduce each risk, such as less data or shorter storage.
You record the remaining risk and decide whether the project may go ahead.
You review the assessment again when the project or the data changes.
beginner.example: Picture a shared flat where the flatmates want a camera in the hallway. Before buying it, they talk the idea through together. Why do they want it? Who will watch the recordings, and for how long? Could a visitor feel watched or be identified unfairly? They decide to point the camera only at the front door. They will keep recordings for one week and tell every visitor. They write these choices on a note beside the door. That talk changed the plan before any money was spent. It has the shape of a privacy impact assessment.
takeaways: Run the assessment before the project starts, not after launch.
Write down real risks, not a list that claims there is no problem.
Use the findings to change the design, and keep the record.

objectives: Explain what a Data Protection Impact Assessment is and when one is needed.
Describe the sections that a useful assessment record should contain.
Identify processing activities that are likely to require a formal assessment.
Explain how a residual risk decision is reached and recorded.
Describe why the assessment must run early enough to change a design.
